1:
Elihu opens the chapter's hymn with his own body as the first witness to the storm, his heart trembling and moved out of its place at the majesty gathering in the sky; and the interpreters agree that a real tempest is rising as he speaks. The reformed John Gill hears in the words a trembling not of terror only but of reverence at the greatness and majesty of God, such as makes all rational creatures — nations, kings, and even the devils — shake before him; he recalls that at the giving of the law the blaze of lightning and the claps of thunder made not only the camp of Israel tremble but Moses himself exceedingly fear and quake. It is very probable, Gill adds, that at this moment Elihu saw a storm gathering and a tempest rising, some flashes of lightning already seen and some murmurs of thunder heard, which began to affect him.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the thunder and lightning as sensible indications of the glory and majesty, the power and terror, of Almighty God — the one addressed to the ear, the other to the eye, the two learning senses. In these, he says, God leaves not himself without witness of his greatness, as in the rain and fruitful seasons he leaves not himself without witness of his goodness (Acts 14:17). Though there are natural causes the philosophers account for, these seem chiefly designed by the Creator to startle and awaken the slumbering world to the consideration of a God above them; and because it thundered and lightened as Elihu spoke — he speaks of the phenomena as present — these were, as afterwards on Mount Sinai, the proper prefaces to the voice of God that would soon break out at ch. 38:1.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke agrees that a proper consideration of God's majesty in the thunder is enough to appall the stoutest heart and fill all with humility and devotion; he complains only that the chapter division is absurd, this passage to the middle of v.5 being a continuation of the account begun at the close of the previous chapter. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott keeps the sense plain and vivid, hearing Elihu say that not only are the cattle terrified, but at this also his heart trembles and is moved out of its place: "Hark! listen to the sound of His voice." The voices do not divide; together they set the storm before us as the visible preface to the God who is about to speak.
2:
From his own trembling Elihu turns to command his hearers, bidding them hear attentively the noise of God's voice and the sound that goes out of his mouth; and the witnesses take the thunder itself as that voice. The reformed John Gill understands the voice of God in the clouds, the thunder that is his voice, and reads Elihu, affected with it himself, as exhorting the company about him to hearken and listen and learn something from it. The wesleyan-arminian voices insist the scene is no metaphor but a present storm. Adam Clarke renders the doubled Hebrew "hear with hearing," and takes it to mean that a violent tempest was actually breaking over the house, the successive peals rolling and the lightning flashing before their eyes; the storm, he says, continued until Elihu had finished, and out of it the Almighty spoke at the opening of the next chapter. The "noise of his voice" he makes the sudden clap, and the "sound that goeth out" the peal or continued rattling that follows to the end. John Wesley agrees it is probable that while Elihu was speaking it thundered, and that this occasioned his return to the subject; the thunder is called God's voice because by it God speaks to the children of men to make them fear before him, and it is said to go out of his mouth because it is produced by his word and command.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch supply the philology and a fine cross-reference. The combination can signify both a constant hearing and, as here, an attentive one; the repetition of the word "voice" five times over these verses calls to mind the sevenfold voice of the LORD that peals through Psalm 29. They note that the demonstrative points not to a storm merely imagined but to that which is now to be perceived by the senses, and they are willing to grant that a copyist may well have added here the observation that the lightning flashes and the thunder rolls. The doubled verb, "hear, O hear," they take not as a mere idiom of emphasis but as a summons to attentive hearing, the same construction that elsewhere bids a man mark and lay to heart what is said; and the "murmur that goeth out of his mouth" they render as the low, continuous rumble that trails the crash, so that the whole peal, from the first clap to its dying growl, is reckoned the utterance of God.

The witnesses converge: whether they weigh the grammar or the gathering weather, they hear in this verse a preacher who will not let his audience treat the thunder as common noise, but presses them to listen, as to a word from God, to the very peals breaking over their heads. It is the same impulse that will move Elihu, a few verses on, to bid Job himself stand still and consider; here he asks only that the company give the storm the attention its Author deserves, and hear in the thunder not weather but a voice.
3:
The reach of the storm becomes the theme as Elihu says God directs it under the whole heaven and sends his lightning to the ends of the earth; and the witnesses marvel at a power that governs what looks to us like chance. The reformed John Gill has God's voice of thunder roll from one end of heaven to the other, charging the clouds and directing both them and it where to discharge — what tree or house or man the bolt shall strike, and where the rain shall fall when the clouds burst — over against the atheism of Pliny, who called thunder and lightning mere chance. Gill cannot resist his homiletic turn: so the ministers of the word, who are themselves compared to clouds, are charged by the Lord with what they shall say and directed where it shall fall with power, even into the very hearts of men, where it pierces as a discerner of their thoughts.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fixes on the speed of the thing. God directs the lightning under the whole heaven in the twinkling of an eye from east to west, and its light — the reflection of the flash, not the bolt itself — reaches the ends of the earth, so that a whole hemisphere seems to see it in the same instant. John Wesley reads the directing more personally: God guides his voice like an arrow to the mark, that it may do the very work for which he sends it, and nothing is left to accident.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott offers a small correction of sense, preferring "sendeth it forth" and referring the "it" to the noise and rumbling that fills all heaven rather than to the bolt alone. But the schools do not really divide. Whether they weigh the flash that outraces the eye or the peal that fills the sky, whether they read the pronoun of the lightning or of the roar, they agree that the vast and instantaneous sweep of the storm — east to west, heaven to earth's ends — is no wild and ungoverned thing but is aimed and dispatched by a hand that appoints its every stroke. What seems to us most casual and unruly, the sudden fork of fire darting where it will, is to Elihu and his expositors the clearest proof of a providence that misses nothing and directs all, so that not a flash escapes the counsel that flung it forth.
4:
The order of the storm — first the flash, then the roar — occupies the witnesses as Elihu says that after the lightning a voice roars, that God thunders with the voice of his excellency, and that he will not stay them when his voice is heard. The reformed John Gill explains the sequence by our senses: after the lightning comes the violent clap, like the roaring of a lion; and though in nature the flash and the report are together, we see before we hear because the sense of seeing is quicker, and the motion of light quicker than that of sound. The roaring voice of thunder becomes for him an emblem of the thunder of the law and of the alarming, awakening sound of the gospel, preached by the sons of thunder (Mark 3:17), by which sinners asleep in trespasses are made to hear and live.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke lingers on "the voice of his excellency," which he renders "of his majesty," declaring that no sound in nature is more descriptive of, or more becoming to, the majesty of God than thunder: we hear the breeze rustle and the cataract dash, but we hear God himself in the continued peal. He then reads "he will not stay them" as meaning that God has not limited or circumscribed the lightnings — they light the whole world, and to them he has assigned no bounds, so that, like God, they are irresistible. Clarke also turns aside to the practical art of measuring a storm's distance by counting the seconds between the flash and the clap, assuring the timid that lightning some seconds off has never been known to do harm.

Here the witnesses genuinely part over the last clause. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott takes "he stayeth them not" the other way: none can track the thunder and the lightning when God's voice is heard, for they travel in paths that none can explore — vivid as the lightning is, who shall pursue its course? The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry offers yet a third sense, that God does not need to check them or hold them back lest they grow unruly, but lets them take their course, saying to them Go, and they go; or else that he will not stay the rains and showers that usually follow the thunder, but pours them out when his voice is heard. So the clause is read three ways — as the lightnings unbounded, as the lightnings untraceable, or as the storm loosed to run its appointed course — a small knot in the grammar over which the schools quietly divide, while agreeing that the whole scene declares a power let loose at God's word and answerable to no other.
5:
Elihu gathers the whole description into a confession of mystery: God thunders marvellously with his voice, doing great things that we cannot comprehend. The reformed John Gill takes "marvellously" to point at the marvellous effects of the thunderbolt — rending rocks and mountains, throwing down strong towers, shattering the mightiest oaks and cedars — and he heaps up the stranger reports that so struck the older naturalists: an egg consumed and its shell left whole, the liquor in a cask spoiled and the cask untouched, money melted in a purse that was not burnt, the child killed in the womb and the mother preserved. Such things, he says, can be accounted for only by the swift and penetrating motion of the lightning; and so, he adds, the voice of God in the gospel thunders out many wonderful things — the Trinity of persons, the everlasting love of the three, the union of two natures in the person of Christ, redemption and salvation by him.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke treats the verse as the true conclusion of Elihu's storm-piece, insisting once more that the account should have closed here, where the description of the thunder and lightning that began at the end of the previous chapter properly ends. He suspects the writer of the book had before him a description like the psalmist's, and sets beside it the great thunderstorm of Psalm 77:16-19, where the waters saw God and were afraid, the clouds poured out water, and the voice of his thunder was in the heaven. The words "great things doeth he," Clarke observes, begin a fresh paragraph, opening onto the wonders of snow and frost and cloud that follow.

The witnesses do not divide. Both read the verse as the hinge of the speech, the point at which the sheer spectacle of the storm is made to yield its lesson: that the God whose voice does such marvels in the sky must be granted to do great things beyond our understanding in his providence as well. Gill's catalogue of prodigies and Clarke's psalm are two ways of pressing the same conclusion — that a power which can melt the coin and spare the purse, which can shake the earth with a word, is not to be arraigned by creatures who cannot so much as trace how the bolt does its work. What we cannot comprehend in the thunder we must be content not to comprehend in the ways of God, and to worship where we cannot follow, so that the confession "we cannot comprehend" is offered less as a complaint than as the beginning of reverence.
6:
"For he saith to the snow, Be thou on the earth" — and the witnesses hear in that bare command a whole doctrine of providence governing the winter weather. The reformed John Gill dwells on the Hebrew that reads literally "be thou earth," out of which one rabbi spun the fancy that the earth was created from snow beneath the throne of glory, a notion Gill, following Maimonides and Aben Ezra, sets aside as resting on a missing letter. The snow he counts among the great and incomprehensible works of God: how it is generated so near us in the lower air and yet so cold, how a thing so cold should warm the earth like a blanket, how it falls even in the hot countries of Africa and yet lies unmelted on the burning top of Etna.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes the verse a rebuke of our irreligious talk about the weather. The changes and extremities of the weather are the subject of much of our common talk, yet how seldom do we speak of them, as Elihu does, with an awful regard to God who directs them. To the snow God says, Be thou on the earth, commissioning it where to light and how long to lie; when he speaks the small rain distils and the great rain pours as he pleases, for saying and doing are not two things with God. It is sin and folly, Henry warns, to contend with God's providence in the weather; if he send the snow or rain, can we hinder them, or shall we be angry at them?

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke turns naturalist, describing how the vapours condense and freeze into crystalline flakes, each a six-pointed star with collateral points set at equal angles, and how the whiteness comes not from any nitrous or fertilizing salt but from the division of the light on countless small surfaces; the snow's whole use, he says, is to cover the tender plants and keep the earth's heat from escaping, so that in northern lands it is an especial blessing of Providence. He even reshapes the verse with Mr. Good, "Behold, he saith to the snow, Be! On earth then falleth it." John Wesley, of the same school, glosses the "great rain of his strength" as the storms of rain that come with great force and irresistible violence. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott keeps it simplest of all: every operation of nature — the snow, the gentle shower, the drenching downpour — obeys the behest of God, who by them seals up the hand of every man that all whom he has made may learn they are not the free agents they suppose. The witnesses converge on a single lesson: that the falling snow, so common we scarcely mark it, is as truly at God's word as the thunder, and preaches the same submission.
7:
What the snow and rain accomplish among men is Elihu's next point: God seals up the hand of every man, that all men may know his work. The reformed John Gill reads the sealing as a shutting up of labour — by deep snows and heavy rains the traveller is stopped, the craftsman hindered, and above all the husbandman kept from his fields, his hands as it were closed and sealed so that he cannot work. He notes Sephorno's gentler turn, that the increase of the earth is brought by the snow and rain into men's hands, leading them to observe the work of God and so to love and fear him.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set the verse at the head of the winter panel that runs on through the frost and the clouds, giving the plain sense that God so binds men's activity that all may be brought to acknowledge his doing; they linger, as their manner is, over the difficult word that the older versions divided between "chosen," "grain," and "brightness," preferring with Schultens to keep it near its root. The wesleyan-arminian witnesses read the sealing of the hand as the work of the frost. Adam Clarke takes it that when the earth is bound up by intense cold the labour of every man is sealed up, and he can do no more in the field until a thaw comes with the south wind; meanwhile the beasts withdraw, some sleeping out the winter in torpor. John Wesley says simply that by these snows and rains God drives men out of the fields and binds their hands from work, that they may seriously contemplate his great and glorious works.

Clarke cannot forbear one indignant digression: on this very verse, he marvels, the whole folly of chiromancy has been built — that God has so marked the lines of every man's hand as to foretell his fortune, and has done it that all men, reading their palms, may know his work — and he points to the great folio that a learned man of Cologne once filled with the fantasy. But the witnesses do not divide over the verse itself. Whether the hand is sealed by snow or by frost, whether men are driven indoors from the plough or the ship, all agree that the enforced idleness of winter has a design in it: that men, taken off from their own business, may attend to God's, and that the very weather which stops their work is meant to open their hearts to the Worker. The rest imposed by the storm is not empty; it is a summons to consider him whose hand has sealed their own.
8:
The withdrawal of the beasts answers the sealing of men's hands, as Elihu observes that then the beasts go into dens and remain in their places. With only two witnesses attending closely, the reading is brief but of one mind. The reformed John Gill takes it of the wild beasts, which, when the snow and rain lie thick upon the earth and they can no longer prowl abroad, betake themselves to their dens, where they lurk and lie in wait for whatever prey may pass. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott draws the parallel that gives the verse its point: not man only, but the beasts likewise, must take refuge in their dens and coverts when the weather drives them in.

The larger sense the witnesses leave to the frame Elihu has been building, and which the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry had drawn out in surveying these verses together. The extremity of the winter weather obliges both men and beasts to retire, making it uncomfortable and unsafe to be abroad. The wild beasts, being wild, must shift for a shelter of their own, and by instinct are directed to it; the tame beasts that serve man are housed and protected by his care, as when the cattle were brought in from the hail of Exodus 9:20. Nature, Henry observes, directs all the creatures to shelter themselves from the storm — and shall man alone be without an ark, unprovided with a refuge when the tempest of God's judgment gathers?

So the little verse, which seems only to note the habits of animals in bad weather, is made to carry the argument forward. The beasts creeping to their dens are one more instance of the whole creation bowing to the command that governs the snow and the frost; each thing keeps the place and the season appointed it, and the wild lion in its lair is as obedient to the winter as the farmer whose plough stands idle. The witnesses do not divide. They read in the retreat of the beasts the same lesson they found in the sealing of the hand: that the storm which shuts up the field and empties the road is no disorder but a discipline, bending every living thing to its Maker's will. And if the brute creation, without reason, knows to seek its covert when the sky darkens, the reasonable creature is the more without excuse who will not seek his shelter in the God whose voice the thunder is. The order Elihu traces in the animal world is set, silently, as a reproach and a call to the man who alone among the creatures forgets to take refuge.
9:
The winds divide the year between them in Elihu's account: out of the south comes the whirlwind, and cold out of the north. Yet the witnesses find the first line less settled than it looks, for the word rendered "south" is properly a hidden inner place. The reformed John Gill lays out the choices: it may be "from the chamber," the inside of the cloud, as Ben Gersom took it, or from the treasury out of which God brings the wind; but because Scripture speaks of the chambers of the south, and the southern pole was to the ancients a secret and unseen region, he is content to render it "south," from which quarter these countries knew the whirlwinds to come. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke refers back to his note on the constellations of Job 9:9, where the same word is rendered "chambers," and reports the Chaldee's "from the supreme chamber shall the commotion come, and from the cataracts of Arcturus the cold"; the whirlwind itself, he thinks, may have been a wind peculiar to that land, a scorching blast something like the simoom.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott agrees, rendering it "out of its chamber cometh the whirlwind," the typhoon, and "cold from the northern constellations," from the quarter of heaven where they shine. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry presses the reading furthest against the received text: the whirlwind, he says, comes out of the hidden place, turning round so that it is hard to say from which point it blows, and he is unwilling to understand this of the south precisely because Elihu says at v.17 that the south wind is no whirlwind at all but a warming and quieting one.

So a genuine difference runs beneath the verse: whether the storm-wind rises "out of the south," as the Authorized reading and Gill allow, or "out of the chamber," the secret storehouse of the winds, as Clarke, Ellicott, and Henry variously prefer. The dispute is not idle, for on it hangs whether the two winds of the verse are simply the hot south and the cold north, or the mysterious hidden blast set over against the freezing north. Yet the witnesses agree on what the antithesis teaches. The same God who keeps the whirlwind in its chamber and looses it at will sends also the cold out of the north; the winds that seem to us to wander where they list are drawn, warm and cold alike, from the storehouses of him who commands them. Whether from the south or from the secret place, the wind goes only where he sends it.
10:
The frost is traced to its true cause as Elihu says that by the breath of God frost is given, and the breadth of the waters is straitened. The reformed John Gill reads "the breath of God" as his word and command — at his bidding the frost appears and at his pleasure it goes — but he allows also the more literal sense of a freezing wind, since the breath of God's nostrils is elsewhere the wind, and the divine name added to a thing enlarges it, so that "the breath of God" may mean a mighty, strong, north wind, as Sephorno took it. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley keeps to the effect: the waters that before spread themselves freely are congealed and bound up in crystal fetters.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke, ever the natural philosopher, owns that the freezing of water, though carefully examined by the ablest minds, is still wrapped in mystery, and is a very proper subject to be reckoned among the great things God does which we cannot comprehend. He marvels at the expansive power of the freezing, which will split a solid gun-barrel and rend a bombshell nearly two inches thick, and he notes that the operation needs the wind, for water lying low did not freeze until a breath of air ruffled its surface, when it shot at once into ice. On the second clause he weighs Mr. Good's rendering, "the expanse of the waters into a mirror," the same word being rendered "melted" at v.18, and describing the frozen surface as a molten glass.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott takes the straitening of the waters' breadth in the same direction, glossing it "firm, like a molten mass" — the broad and flowing water arrested and made solid at a breath. The witnesses do not divide, though they weigh the "breath of God" differently, some hearing in it the bare word of command and others the freezing north wind that carries out the word. What they hold in common is the wonder that a thing so hard and so vast — a river or a lake locked into ice — should be done by so soft a thing as a breath, and done so silently that, were it not common, it would seem next to a miracle. The God whose thunder shakes the heavens needs no thunder to bind the waters; he has only to breathe, and the flood stands still. And in that quiet, effortless mastery Elihu finds a power as awful, in its way, as the storm — the power that turns the running stream to stone with a whisper.
11:
The clouds themselves come under Elihu's eye, and the verse — "also by watering he wearieth the thick cloud; he scattereth his bright cloud" — proves one of the knottiest in the chapter, the witnesses dividing over the very verb. The reformed John Gill takes the plain reading: by filling the cloud with a multitude of waters God loads and as it were wearies it, sending it about laden like a tired traveller and then draining it of its rain until it is spent — a fit emblem, he adds, of the ministers who spend and are spent for the good of men; though he knows that some render the word by serenity or fair weather, as Mr. Broughton did. John Wesley, another wesleyan-arminian voice, reads it the same way: the clouds spend themselves and are wearied watering the earth and journeying to distant parts to empty themselves, and the bright lightsome clouds God scatters and dissolves by the wind or sun.

Against this the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke prefers a wholly different sense, that "the brightness dissipates the cloud" — the bright sunshine wearing out and dispersing the thick cloud — though he allows the received rendering that by watering the earth God empties the cloud of all its contents; and he records the Vulgate's turn, that the grain longs for the clouds and the clouds scatter abroad their light. The grammatical-historical witnesses hold both possibilities open. Charles Ellicott gives first "He ladeth the thick cloud with moisture" and "scattereth the cloud of his lightning," but sets beside it the alternative that "the bright sun weareth out and disperseth the thick cloud." Keil and Delitzsch, weighing the same doubtful word, render the line "He loadeth the clouds with water, he spreadeth far and wide the cloud of his light."

So the verse is read in three directions at once: that God wearies the cloud by watering the earth from it, that he wearies or wears out the cloud by the bright sun that disperses it, or that he loads the cloud with moisture and spreads his lightning-cloud abroad. The difference is real, turning on whether the cloud is being emptied, dispersed, or filled. Yet the witnesses agree on the governing thought that Elihu is after: whichever way the words run, it is God who charges the cloud and God who discharges it, God who loads it with rain and God who sweeps it clean. The vapours that seem to drift at the wind's caprice are handled, filled, and emptied at his will, and the very obscurity of the grammar only underscores how far the workings of the sky lie beyond the reckoning of the man Elihu is instructing.
12:
Elihu follows the cloud through its wanderings: it is turned round about by God's counsels, that it may do whatsoever he commands upon the face of the world. The reformed John Gill reads it of the cloud driven by the wind, which is turned about to every point of the compass according to the will of God, who sits as it were at the helm and orders all things by the counsel of his own will; to that counsel he traces every shifting of the wind and every motion of the clouds. John Wesley, of the wesleyan-arminian school, says the same in fewer words: the clouds are carried about to this place or that, not by chance — though nothing seems more casual than their motions — but by God's order and governance.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch take the verse as the turn toward Job's instruction, where the man who would dictate to God is bidden rather to stand still and read God's wonders in the sky, that the clouds execute all he commands them over the wide earth. Here the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke strikes out on a path of his own. Finding the Hebrew difficult, he paraphrases the verse of the sun rather than the cloud: the sun makes its revolutions, turning round upon its own axis, and by its attachments — its attractive and repulsive influences, as by a strong cable — holds the heavenly bodies in their courses and projects them to their proper distances. That men "may do whatsoever he commandeth them" he then reads of men availing themselves of sun and season to cultivate the earth. Yet Clarke is honest enough to add that this exposition may be too far-fetched, and that the passage perhaps refers only to the revolutions of the seasons.

So the verse is read chiefly of the cloud, wheeled about the sky by the counsels of God to carry out his errands of rain — whether, as the next verse will say, for correction or for mercy. Clarke's astronomical excursion stands apart as the one voice that would make the sun and its orbits the subject, and even he half-retracts it. The witnesses do not finally divide; they agree that the point of the verse is not the mechanism but the government — that the clouds, however they turn and drift, are steered by a wisdom that bends them to a purpose, so that not a shower falls at random but each is dispatched to the very spot and for the very end that God's counsel has fixed. The wandering cloud is on an errand, and the hand that turns it is the same that rules the world.
13:
The errand of the rain is named at last: God causes it to come, whether for correction, or for his land, or for mercy. The reformed John Gill notes only, and simply, that it is the cloud and its rain that God thus causes to come; the weight of the verse the other witnesses carry. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke unfolds the three ends with care. The rain is sent "for correction" — the word meaning a rod or scourge — when God inundates a land and sweeps away its produce in irresistible floods; "for his land," that is for Palestine, the place of his favoured people; and "for mercy," when a district wasted by locusts or drought is restored by fertilizing showers, and the desert made to blossom. He gives too the Vulgate's reading, that God commands the clouds to be found "whether in one tribe, or in his own land, or in whatsoever place of his mercy," and recalls how some have thought Elihu glances here at the flood of the old world.

John Wesley, of the same wesleyan-arminian school, divides the verse the same way. "Correction" is the scourging of men by immoderate showers; "his earth" he takes broadly of the whole earth, which is the Lord's, so that the clause may reach even to the universal deluge that came in great measure out of the clouds; and "mercy" is for the benefit of mankind, the cooling of the air and the improving of the fruits of the ground. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, surveying these verses, had pressed the moral that the two witnesses only imply: the very same rain, according to the measure in which it is given, may be either a great judgment or a great mercy, so that God makes it fall, as the prophet says, on one city and not on another (Amos 4:7), for the correction of his land or for its blessing.

The witnesses do not divide. They agree that the rain is never a merely natural event but always a moral errand, sent with intent — to chastise, to preserve, or to bless — and that the same drops which drown one field ripen another. What looks to the farmer like the luck of the weather is to Elihu the discriminating hand of God, weighing out judgment and mercy in the fall of a shower. And here the long survey of snow and frost and cloud reaches its purpose, for if God so governs the rain toward men, correcting some and sparing others by the same means, then Job's own affliction, like the rain, may be either a scourge or a mercy — a thought Elihu will press directly upon him in the verse that follows.
14:
The sweep of the storm turns now upon Job himself, as Elihu breaks off to say, "Hearken unto this, O Job; stand still, and consider the wondrous works of God." The reformed John Gill hears the summons pointed either at the present clap of thunder or, more likely, at what Elihu has just said of the clouds that come for correction or for mercy: Job is to apply it to his own case and consider whether the afflictions upon him are for his reproof or in love to his soul, since both, Gill allows, might be so. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sharpens each verb — hear what is said on the part of God; stand still, and enter into deep contemplation; consider, weighing every thing separately and together — and dwells on the phrase "wondrous works," endless in variety, stupendous in structure, and incomprehensible in the mode of their making. John Wesley adds the argument from the lesser to the greater: if there be so much matter of wonder in the most obvious works of God, how wonderful must his secret counsels be.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes the verse the doorway to all that follows and unfolds its "stand still." What we hear is not likely to profit us unless we consider it, he says, and we are not likely to consider things fully unless we stand still and compose ourselves to it; the works of God, being wondrous, both deserve and need our consideration, and the due consideration of them will help to reconcile us to all his providences. Elihu's whole design, on Henry's reading, is the humbling of Job: to show him that he had no insight into the natural causes of things, no share in the first making of the world, and no words fit to speak of the glory of God, so that a man so ignorant of the divine mechanics is no competent judge of the divine politics.

The witnesses do not divide. They agree that the storm has not been described for its own sake but to bring Job to a halt — to stop his pleading long enough to look, and by looking to be humbled. The command is gentle and grave at once: not to argue, not to answer, but to stand still and consider. And in that pause Elihu means to lodge the whole force of his argument, that the God whose common works of snow and cloud already outrun our understanding is not to be called to account by a sufferer who cannot explain the weather. Job is bidden to let the wonders he cannot fathom teach him patience with the providence he cannot fathom, and to find, in standing still, the beginning of his peace.
15:
Elihu begins his catechism of Job's ignorance with the clouds: "Dost thou know when God disposed them, and caused the light of his cloud to shine?" The reformed John Gill takes the clouds as the wondrous works in view — when God decreed them, stored them with rain and hail and snow, disposed them through the heavens, and ordered them where to fall — and asks whether Job was present at all this and knew beforehand what would break out of them; and if he was ignorant of these things, how should he imagine himself acquainted with the secret springs of God's providential dealings with men? The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch keep the clause temporal, "dost thou know when God disposed them," setting Job before a work whose timing he can neither foresee nor explain.

Over "the light of his cloud" the witnesses divide. The wesleyan-arminian voices read it of the rainbow. Adam Clarke reports that almost every critic of note understands the phrase of the bow God gave as the sign that the earth should be no more destroyed by water (Genesis 9:13), and John Wesley agrees that it is probably the rainbow, seated in a cloud that may well be called God's cloud because in it he set his bow. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott takes it rather of the lightning, as before — "dost thou know all the secrets of God's thunderbolts, at whom and how he will use them?" — though he records the further guess that it means the sun, and asks whether Job knows how God uses the sun to disperse the clouds.

So the phrase is read three ways — as the rainbow arched in the cloud, as the lightning hidden in it, or as the sunlight that scatters it — a small but real difference in what token of God's power is here set before Job. Yet the witnesses agree on the thrust of the question. Whether the light be the bow of the covenant, the bolt of the storm, or the sun behind the vapours, Job knows neither the time of its shining nor the counsel that appoints it. Elihu is not asking him to admire a phenomenon but to measure his own ignorance: a man who cannot tell when or why the light breaks from the cloud is in no position to sit in judgment on the dealings of the God who orders it. The catechism has begun, and its every question is designed to bring the same answer from Job's lips — that he does not know.
16:
The catechism presses on to a marvel nearer to hand, the poise of the clouds themselves: does Job know the balancings of the clouds, the wondrous works of him who is perfect in knowledge? The reformed John Gill puts the wonder as a question of weight — how those ponderous bodies, some of them very heavy and full of water, are so poised that they hang in the air without tilting one way or another and without falling upon the earth. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sets the same wonder in the language of his own science: does Job understand evaporation, and the gravity of the air at different heights, well enough to say how the atmosphere bears up such different weights of watery vapour, keeping them afloat for a season and then letting them down to water the ground? He prefers Mr. Good's rendering of the closing phrase, an exclamation rather than a paraphrase — "Wonders, perfections of wisdom!"

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott lets a poet carry the thought, glossing the balancings as the way the clouds are poised and suspended in the sky, and quoting Coleridge's line, "Ye clouds, that far above me float and pause." John Wesley, of the wesleyan-arminian school, keeps to the plain figure: God does as it were weigh the clouds in his balances, so that, full of water though they are, they are held up by the thin and yielding air. The witnesses do not divide.

What they marvel at together is the improbability of the thing — that so much water should be hung over our heads on nothing, kept from falling all at once and yet made to fall in due measure. The cloud that seems the very image of what is unstable and fleeting is in truth a work of exact balance, weighed and suspended by a wisdom that never miscalculates; and Elihu presses the point home by naming its author "perfect in knowledge." The clouds are the standing proof that God's understanding has no flaw, for a hair's breadth of error in their poising would drown the world or parch it. Job, who cannot so much as explain how the least of them is held aloft, is asked to bow before a knowledge that balances them all. The question is not meant to shame him for being no philosopher, but to lift his eyes from his own dark case to the flawless wisdom that governs even the water in the sky, and to trust it where he cannot trace it.
17:
Elihu turns from the winter sky to the sultry heat, asking Job how his garments grow warm upon him when God quiets the earth by the south wind. The reformed John Gill grants that there seems no great difficulty here — a man's clothes are warm, and himself so hot in the summer season, when only the south wind blows and brings a serene sky, that he can scarcely bear them — and yet, he insists, there is a concourse of divine Providence attending these natural causes, and a divine blessing with them, without which the garment would not warm the man at all. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke turns the simple question into a confession of how little we know: what, after all, are warmth and cold? He doubts whether the very existence of heat as a substance, or of cold as the mere absence of it, is truly settled, and explains that our garments keep us warm only by hindering the escape of our natural heat, wool and the like being poor conductors; yet why the north wind should bring cold and the south wind heat, he owns, is to him not demonstrated. John Wesley reads the quieting more narrowly of the air, made calm and warm by the sun's coming into the southern quarter.

The grammatical-historical witnesses attend to the grammar. Charles Ellicott offers the alternative "when the earth is still," taking the clause of the sultry calm rather than of the wind's agency; and Keil and Delitzsch, reading the Hebrew particle as "that" rather than "how," would carry the sentence on into the next verse, addressing Job as the man "whose garments became hot when the land is sultry from the south." The witnesses do not divide over the picture — the oppressive warmth of a still, south-blown day — but weigh differently how the clause is joined and how far the wonder is to be pressed.

What they share is the shrewdness of Elihu's choice. He does not ask about some rare prodigy but about the plainest daily experience, the heat of one's own clothes on a warm day, precisely to show that even here Job cannot reach the bottom of things. The commonest sensation, felt on the skin, hides a mystery the wisest cannot open; and if the warmth of a garment defeats our understanding, how much more the dealings of God. Elihu is narrowing the ground beneath Job's feet, taking away even the ordinary and familiar as a place to stand and dispute, and leaving him only the confession that he does not know.
18:
From the heat of the day Elihu lifts Job's eyes to the vault above it: "Hast thou with him spread out the sky, which is strong, and as a molten looking glass?" The reformed John Gill takes the question as a challenge to Job's presumption — was he concerned in the first spreading out of the sky, an assistant in the work? Surely not; God spread it as a curtain and canopy about himself, without the help of another. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley draws out the paradox in the description: the sky, though thin and transparent, is yet firm and compact and steadfast; and the "molten looking glass," the mirrors of that age being made of polished brass and steel, is smooth and without the least flaw, a glass in which, as the psalmist says, we may behold the glory of God and the wisdom of his handiwork.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke turns the verse into a hymn to the fitness of the world. Was Job with God when he made the expanse, fitted the weight to the winds, proportioned the sea to the land, and gave the air its gravity and elasticity, without which neither animal nor plant could live? The whole concave of heaven, in a clear day or a bright night, is like a mass of polished metal, reflecting and transmitting innumerable images. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott would render it "hast thou spread out with him the magnificent dome of heaven," and notes that the words used imply the cloud-covered rather than the cloudless sky, so that it is not impossible the sun is still the hidden subject of these verses.

Keil and Delitzsch, the other grammatical-historical witness, hearing the whole final strophe begin here, draw the moral that binds it to what has gone before: he who censures God's actions and murmurs against him injures himself, whereas a patient waiting on him would be richly rewarded. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that the firmament, at once so delicate and so enduring, so vast and so brightly finished, is a work in which Job had no part and can claim no share, and that to have had no hand in the making of the world is to have no standing to arraign its government. The mirror of the sky, spread out by God alone and polished without a flaw, throws back upon the man who looks up at it the image of his own smallness; and Elihu means that the sight should silence him, teaching him to adore where he cannot advise, and to leave the ordering of a world he never helped to build in the hands that stretched out the heavens.
19:
Having shown Job his ignorance of the heavens, Elihu includes himself and his fellows in it: "Teach us what we shall say unto him; for we cannot order our speech by reason of darkness." The reformed John Gill reads it as a confession of how ill men are fitted to reason with the wonder-working God about his providence, when they know so little even of his common works in nature; let Job, who is so eager to plead, tell them how it should be done. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke hears in it a strong and biting irony aimed at Job's pretensions: thou who art so wise, make us as wise as thyself, that we too may approach the Sovereign of the world with thy boldness and maintain our cause before him — for our part, we are ignorant, and on all these things are wrapped in darkness. He notes Mr. Good's rendering, which turns the darkness upon God rather than upon us: "teach us how we may address him, when arrayed in robes of darkness." John Wesley makes the darkness double — the darkness of the matter, since God's counsels are a great deep, and the darkness of our own minds — so that we cannot maintain any discourse with him.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott keeps to the thread that runs through his reading of these verses, taking the "him" to be the sun, hidden altogether by the clouds: is he gone, or is he not still there behind them? On Ellicott's reckoning the verse is of a piece with a meditation on the obscured sun, which he will carry to the chapter's close. But the other witnesses take the "him" to be God, and the darkness to be the mind's inability to frame fit words about him.

The witnesses do not finally divide over the lesson, whatever they make of the pronoun. All agree that the verse is a rebuke to the confidence with which Job had proposed to reason his case with the Almighty. Elihu, who has spoken so long and so well on God's behalf, will not claim to be able to order a single speech to him without being lost in darkness; and if the advocate is thus baffled, how much more the man who would be plaintiff against God. The irony is grave beneath its sting: Job had asked for a hearing before God, and Elihu answers that no man living, himself included, can so much as arrange his words in that presence. The darkness Elihu confesses is not ignorance to be ashamed of but the proper condition of a creature before his Maker, and the honest owning of it is the beginning of wisdom.
20:
Elihu shrinks back from his own boldness in the next breath: "Shall it be told him that I speak? if a man speak, surely he shall be swallowed up." The reformed John Gill hears a man asking whether anything he has said is worth relating to the God who is already omniscient, or worth his hearing, being so imperfect; and above all whether it should ever be reported to God that Elihu had spoken as Job did, arraigning his justice and complaining of his dealings — God forbid, he says, that such words should be laid to his charge. He notes Mr. Broughton's turn, "shall it be recorded unto him that I speak?" — as though a man's presuming to plead God's cause, or Job's, could be entered in a book and sent up to heaven.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke draws the sharp contrast between Elihu's fear and Job's rashness. Shall I dare so much as whisper before God, he asks, and if any accused me for what I have spoken, though well intended, how could I stand? I should be swallowed up in consternation and consumed by the splendour of his majesty. And then he turns upon Job: but in what state art thou, who hast arraigned God's government, found fault with his providence, and all but charged him with cruelty — what will become of thee? John Wesley reads the swallowing up as the effect of God's infinite majesty upon any man bold enough to send a challenge to God or to enter the lists with him.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott allows the sense to vary with the subject: taken of God, it is a simple expression of awe — "shall it be told him that I would speak? if a man speak, surely he shall be swallowed up"; but taken of the sun, of which he has been discoursing, it becomes the question whether any man ever ventured to say that the sun is swallowed up and extinguished. The witnesses do not divide over the awe, however they read the figure. They agree that Elihu here measures the distance between himself and God, and finds it so great that even to have spoken well seems a presumption to be half regretted. The lesson for Job is plain and unspoken: if the man who has defended God trembles to think his words reported in heaven, what shall be said of the man who has spoken against him? Elihu's self-effacement is itself a reproof, teaching that the nearer a soul comes to the majesty of God, the less it dares to say, and the more it fears to have said too much.
21:
The gathering darkness of the storm returns as Elihu's theme: now men see not the bright light which is in the clouds, but the wind passes and cleanses them. The reformed John Gill sifts the possibilities and settles on the sun. It is not the lightning, which is not seen until it breaks out, nor the rainbow, which vanishes when the wind clears the cloud, nor the Milky Way that Sephorno suggested, but the great bright light of the sun, sometimes hidden from men by interposing clouds until the wind sweeps them away — or rather, he thinks, the sun shining in its full strength in a clear sky, when men are not able to look full upon it. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it the same way through Mr. Good, "even now we cannot look at the light when it is resplendent in the heavens, and a wind from the north hath passed along and cleared them": who can gaze at the sun blazing in a sky swept clean, much less upon the majesty of God? John Wesley too takes the light for the sun, which men cannot behold when the sky is very clear, and infers that it is no wonder we cannot see God or discern his counsels.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears Elihu, as he draws to a close, watching an actual sky. God, who has said he will dwell in the thick darkness (2 Chron. 6:1), is advancing as in an awful chariot, surrounded with clouds so black over their heads that the bright light just before seen is hidden, which reminded Elihu of the darkness that stopped his speech and made him afraid to go on, as the disciples feared when they entered the cloud (Luke 9:34). Yet Henry sees him look to the north and find it clearing, and take hope that the clouds are not gathering for a deluge but shall be swept by a wind, as the wind passed over the earth to dry the flood of Noah (Gen. 8:1).

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott makes the verse the very threshold of the theophany: the sun is bright behind the clouds, and when the wind, even the north wind, has cleared them, he comes forth like gold — but upon God is terrible majesty; though the hidden sun we shall see again, who shall ever find out God? The witnesses converge: the obscured and re-emerging light becomes a parable of the God who veils himself in the storm and is about to speak from it.
22:
Out of that clearing sky Elihu draws his last images: fair weather comes out of the north, and with God is terrible majesty. But the first clause hides a famous crux, and the witnesses divide over whether it speaks of weather or of gold. The reformed John Gill notes that the word rendered "fair weather" is literally "gold," which some take strictly — gold being found in the northern lands of Colchis and Scythia, north of Palestine — while others, and Gill leans this way, understand it figuratively of the serenity of the air, bright and pure as gold, the "golden weather" of Mr. Broughton's rendering. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the line flatly of the metal, "gold is brought from the north," and set over against it the awful clause, "above Eloah is terrible majesty."

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke defends the literal "gold" at length, asking how "fair weather" can be any version of the Hebrew, which nearly every ancient and modern version renders "from the north cometh gold." With Calmet he observes that in the days of Job and Moses gold came from Colchis, Armenia, and Ophir, all reckoned north countries; and the connection with the terrible majesty of God he finds in this, that as gold, the most precious of metals, comes from the north, so praises offered to God must be accompanied with fear and trembling, terrible majesty belonging to him alone. He records too Mr. Good's bolder emendation, "splendour itself is with God, insufferable majesty," but grants that no ancient version or manuscript supports it. John Wesley, of the same school, keeps to the weather, taking it of the northern winds that scatter the clouds and clear the sky, and hears Elihu now speaking abruptly and in haste because he perceives that God is about to take the work into his own hands.

So the verse is read two ways — as the golden fair weather breaking from the north after the storm, or as the gold that is dug from the northern lands — and the choice is a real one, resting on the same Hebrew word and settled by no version alike. Yet the two readings meet in the clause that crowns the verse: whichever comes out of the north, gold or clear sky, with God is terrible majesty, before which both the treasure and the fair weather are as nothing. The witnesses do not divide over that. Whether Elihu points to the brightening heavens or to the precious metal, he does it only to turn the eye upward to a majesty more dreadful and more golden than either, the majesty of the God who is now about to appear.
23:
"Touching the Almighty, we cannot find him out" — with this Elihu reaches the summit of his praise, confessing a God excellent in power and in judgment and in plenty of justice, who will not afflict. The reformed John Gill dwells on the name Almighty: the God with whom nothing is impossible, who does whatever he pleases and more than we can ask or think, and who is all-sufficient, having enough in himself to make himself blessed and needing nothing his creatures can give. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, drawing these closing verses together, reads the confession as a chain of glories: that we cannot find him out, our finite understanding never comprehending his infinite perfections nor tracing his way in the sea; that he is excellent in power, able to do whatever he pleases in heaven and earth; that he is no less excellent in wisdom and justice, so that he who can do everything will do everything for the best; and that he will not afflict — not willingly, nor without cause, nor beyond what is needful, but always considering our frame.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses press the sense of that last clause in different directions. John Wesley keeps the received reading, that God will not afflict without just cause, and adds that being excellent in power he neither needs nor can do any unrighteous act, for all such things are acts of weakness; in the administration of judgment he never did nor can use his power unjustly, as Job seemed to insinuate. But Adam Clarke breaks with the whole rendering, taking the Hebrew to mean not "he will not afflict" but "he will not answer": the Almighty, whom we cannot find out, gives account of none of his matters to us, and we can no more comprehend his motives and his ends than his being. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott is content to read the verse of a God mighty in power and justice, leaving the crux where he finds it.

So the last clause is read two ways — that God will not afflict beyond just cause, or that God will not answer for his doings to men — and the difference is not slight, for the one comforts the sufferer with God's restraint and the other silences him with God's sovereignty. Yet the witnesses do not divide over the heart of the verse, the great confession that the Almighty cannot be found out. Whether he will not afflict without cause or will not answer at all, the conclusion for Job is the same: that a God so far past our finding out is to be trusted and adored, not arraigned, and that the justice we cannot fathom is justice still.
24:
The hymn ends where all true knowledge of God must end, in fear: men do therefore fear him, and he respecteth not any that are wise of heart. The reformed John Gill gathers the grounds of that fear from all that has gone before — the greatness of God in power and judgment and justice, and his goodness in afflicting men not for his own pleasure but for their profit — and concludes that men should therefore reverence and adore him, submit to his will, bear their afflictions patiently, and serve him with godly fear. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the fear as reverence and humble submission, the opposite of presuming to quarrel or dispute with God, and takes "the wise of heart" whom God does not regard to be those wise in their own eyes.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sharpens the last clause into the humbling of all human pride: therefore let wretched, sinful men fear him, for no man is valuable in God's sight on account of his wisdom, and whatever good is in a man, God alone is the author of it — let him that glorieth, then, glory in the Lord. And Clarke cannot close the chapter without marking the change that is upon them: Elihu, knowing that the Almighty will now speak for himself, has prepared the way by his terrible description of the thunder and lightning; the evidences of the divine presence throng upon his mind, his powers of speech fail him in the darkness, and just then the terrible majesty of the Lord appears, the whirlwind proclaims his presence, and out of it God answers for himself.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott hears in the closing words a play that the ear can catch but the translation cannot keep, between the words for fearing and for seeing, and would render the clause, "therefore men may fear him, but as for the wise in heart, no one even of them shall see him." He grants that the Authorized reading — that God respects not the self-conceited wise — is the more literal, though it seems to him a doubtful sentiment, since God surely does regard the truly wise. The witnesses do not finally divide. Whether the clause means that God pays no court to those who are wise in their own eyes, or that not even the wisest of men shall see him, both readings bow to the same conclusion that crowns Elihu's whole discourse: that the fitting posture of man before this unsearchable God is reverence, and that the beginning and the end of wisdom is to fear him. So the long storm-piece closes, and the stage is cleared, for the God whom Elihu could only point to is about to speak.
